80.t: How Ma Rainey compared as a performer with the Smiths
80.s: Ma was not as dynamic or loud as Bessie or Clara, but was an early Southern star who ran several touring shows that left performers stranded.
80.ch: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
80.q: No. To answer you -- wait just a minute -- to answer you, because when you say electrifying a person will -- bang! -- when those people really start out. Clara Smith, Bessie Smith --

80.t: Bessie Smith versus Clara Smith: rival shows and the club showdown
80.s: When two Smith shows were booked into the same town, the rivals sat at named tables in a club and tried to outdo each other while the master of ceremonies chose who to introduce first.
80.ch: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
80.q: Not her sister, but I mean anybody else who moved in, you know. Oh, you would like this. Bessie, Clara, the two -- lot of people thought they were sisters. But they'd be booked into the same town, quite often. You know, the guys would be booking, put Bessie in this theater, and Clara in the other…

80.s: He first met Ma Rainey in Texas with his show: a plump, light-brown, generous woman with a chain of $20 gold pieces who liked young musicians.
80.ch: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
80.q: I met Ma, I think the first was down in Texas. It was Houston, Texas, I think, and I was with this show that I was telling you about. And Ma was there with her show, and we came -- how we came in contact with each other right now I don't remember, but I can see a picture of her face, a big round…

80.t: Ranking Clara, Mamie and Trixie Smith
80.s: Clara was loud and good but below Bessie, Mamie was nice but never took with the public, and Trixie was mediocre.
80.ch: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
80.q: No, well now Clara was -- Clara was loud, but smaller, and good. Oh yes, she could sing. but I mean she didn't hit the top like Bessie. Everybody liked -- I think Bessie was -- got great buxom voice there, that could go (Sings) We-e-e-l-l, this is Bessie, so and so, you know.

80.t: Ethel Waters calls him on stage to play 'Am I Blue?'
80.s: In Philadelphia Ethel Waters asked her favourite trumpeter in the audience to join her; he borrowed a pit trumpet and used what he learned from Dyer.
80.ch: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
80.q: Yeah, she was -- oh man, what -- and the thing that knocked me out, I was sitting in the theater one night, digging her show. I was in Philadelphia, by the way. She was there with the show -- no, she was there and somebody called out in the audience and sort of come up on stage and be acknowledged…

80.t: Backing Bessie, Clara, Mamie and Trixie Smith at the Howard
80.s: Four or five shows a day, with blues singers as headliners who brought their own comedians and chorus girls but usually only a pianist.
80.q: Aw, man! Let's see. Four or five a day, and it all depends on what they have in there. They had a blues singer in there, you know, one of the Smiths, Bessie Smith, Mamie Smith, but mainly Bessie, and Clara. Clara wasn't bad. She was very good. Trixie Smith. I played for all of them.

176.t: Favorite blues singers: Bessie Smith and Ma Rainey
176.s: Billie says Bessie Smith was her favorite, disliked Ida Cox and Sara Martin, and compares Ma Rainey's heavy voice, recalling first playing for Bessie.
176.q: Bessie Smith. Well, I liked all the rest of them, but Bessie Smith was just most wise. Bessie Smith, I didn't think too much of Ida Cox singing, I worked with Ida. I never didn't like her singing.

176.t: Playing for Bessie Smith in Pensacola
176.s: Billie played Gulf Coast Blues for Bessie Smith in Pensacola when Clarence Williams came through.
176.q: I played the Gulf Coast Blues for Bessie Smith in Pensacola Florida when Clarence Williams came with a된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된

176.s: Billie says Ida Cox and Bessie were her favourites, and she did not care for Ma Rainey.
176.q: Ida Cox was a good singer. You know, I moved on a trip with him after that. Oh yeah, I went on a road with Ida. Well, Ida and Betsy was my best one, the only thing I cared anything about singing. I didn't like Mama Rainey singing. You didn't know anything? I didn't like her singing. Now they like…

176.t: Working on Bessie Smith's show as chorus and pianist
176.s: Billie did chorus work and then played piano when Bessie's pianist Clarence Williams fell ill.
176.q: I did it in the chorus. See, Clarence William, Clarence William got sick, see, he couldn't work no more with her. And by me, I wasn't doing chorus, I could play piano right on, playing piano, that's why I got my style in the chorus, see. Like that.

176.t: Billie's sisters as singers and blues
176.s: The sisters all sang; Edna, Della and Billie loved blues while Sadie and Ida preferred sentimental songs.
176.q: See, they more sing that, uh, channel voice, like you know, all the nice songs, you know, really nice, sentimental songs like that. He didn't sing no variety blues. That's everything I ever did, like singing about blues. Yeah, but I mean Sadie. No, Sadie never sing no blues. Sadie never sing no…

4.t: Mamie Smart before she became Mamie Smith
4.s: Mamie Smart sang with the Troubadours in St. Louis and went East before her Crazy Blues hit.
4.ch: Second session: boyhood, brothers and early road years
4.q: No, she was in St. Louis. She was...you know, joined Bill Bailey's Troubadours, and when that broke up, she went on East, and next time I heard from her--Mamie Smith, and she was a hit on this record 'Crazy Blues.'

4.t: Mamie Smith's background and the Black Swan label with Alberta Hunter
4.s: Spikes had traveled with Mamie Smith in Bill Bailey's show; Alberta Hunter made the first recording of Someday Sweetheart on Black Swan, arranged by Grant Still.
4.q: I think about seventy-five cents...sixty-five or seventy-five cents, then they got up to eighty-five and up to a dollar, I think, and I was going to tell you about Mamie Smith. Her name was Mamie...it's been so long...but we travelled with her, I told you, with Bill Bailey's Troubadours. She was…

4.t: The Crazy Blues record craze at the store
4.s: Mamie Smith's record started a rush; customers lined up around the block for new Bessie and Mamie Smith records priced from sixty-five cents to a dollar.
4.q: Mamie Smith came out with 'Crazy Blues.' That started them, you know. And then we couldn't get enough records, you know, for a year or two. We'd get in fifty or a hundred records, and they'd be gone in an hour. 'Cause we'd put a just sign up on the door out in front: 'Bessie Smith New Record In' or…

4.s: Hazel Myers was the leading singer in Steppin' High; Lucille Hegamin recorded in New York alongside Mamie Smith while her husband played piano.
4.ch: Shows, scripts and the Mosby-era names
4.q: No, Hazel Myers came out, and they were featuring her in "Steppin' High." She was the leading singer in "Steppin' High,"

58.s: Punch explains filling in when the singer cuts out and notes Johnny Dunn's plunger.
58.q: Well, we used to do it. When the singer, singer, say and listen and cut out, we fill in. But now they go right along with the singer, you know what I mean? Like somebody say, I've got the blues and the blues about to kill me. I've got the blues and the blues about to kill me. And if I lose the…

58.t: Blue Island, Big Bill and Ma Rainey
58.s: Punch explains Blue Island, records with Big Bill, and Ma Rainey on the Mac and Mac show.
58.ch: Jelly Roll, Leonard Reed and Chicago mixed crowds
58.q: Well that was, uh, there was a place on there called Blue Island. Did Tony work there or anything? Yeah, Tony worked there. But I wasn't really. I see. But it's a place called Blue Island. Yeah, that's way out south in Chicago, Blue Island. Yeah. Was it a nightclub or a town? It's a town,

58.s: Punch recalls two male singers and no women, and that Lizzie Miles was away.
58.q: Willie Jackson. I don't know what that fellow's name, Snooki Scotty or something Scotty. Them was the only two singers. I knew what they were around here in them time. Snooki Scotty, huh? No, his name was Willie Jackson and Colin. Yes. He worked there, right down there, right there, right there…

706.s: Armstrong describes how he got the accompanying work through Fletcher Henderson and how he filled in behind singers, recalling Bessie Smith writing blues in the studio.
706.q: Yeah, well, I got that break when I was with Fletch Henderson, you know, at the Roadland. Yeah. And we would go down, like, one day to the trombone, the clarinet, and the cornet, then one day, all three of us. Yeah. And the Dixon on the banjo, and we made out a little extra change like that.

706.t: Ma Rainey, Bessie Smith and other blues singers
706.s: Armstrong compares Ma Rainey and Bessie Smith and says he played with all of the blues singers.
706.q: Well, I don't know who was first. R. Rainey had been singing a long time. Became a set gal, you know. Good woman. Yeah, I think Bessie came a little later and out sang them all.

706.t: Blues singers and Ma Rainey's Countin' the Blues
706.s: Gleason introduces a Ma Rainey record; Armstrong says singers like Bessie, Mamie and Clara Smith played theaters rather than Oliver's Lincoln Gardens.
706.q: They didn't. I mean, they're always in the theaters, and the crowd's standing around the corner to get in. Yeah. Like Bessie Smith, Mamie Smith, and Clara Smith, and Miss Barnes, what is her name? She was in, no, she made this good time flat blues. All that. Yeah. Yeah. Well, they always had their…

1.t: Perry Bradford, Mamie Smith and the Smith sisters of the blues
1.s: Danny tells how Perry Bradford got Mamie Smith to record Crazy Blues and launched the rush for blues singers named Smith.
1.ch: Danny's rise through New York bands to Cab Calloway
1.q: Now, the music has got a thing whereby... [SINGS] "I'm Alabama bound, Alabama bound, [HUMS 2 BARS], Leave a dime(?) for beer(?)..." Now, Perry Bradford jumped up and said he wrote that. But you see, Perry Bradford...Mamie Smith... He's the one that introduced Mamie Smith to Columbia...

1.t: Clara Smith and Perry Bradford's recording of Mamie Smith
1.s: Danny recalls Clara Smith's low-down blues, and how the relentless Perry Bradford finally got Crazy Blues recorded; Milt helped bury him. End of Tape 5 side A.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: Clara Smith was a defiant little dark woman. She sang the low-down Blues. There was Clara, and Mamie and Bessie, that trio. Trixie... There was just a whole slew of Smith sisters. As long as you had name Smith, you could put that on the marquee... I don't know if I mentioned it before. They just…

1.t: Victoria Spivey and Sweet Pea Spivey
1.s: Danny recalls Victoria Spivey's hit Mean Black Snake Blues and her sister Sweet Pea.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: called "Mean Black Snake Blues." "Mean black snake's been sucking my (?) down." And that was a terrific hit, and that just threw her up to the top. But she didn't follow up. And she had a sister called Honey...Honey...Honey Somethin'... Sweet Pea Spivey.

67.t: Sophisticated musicians' contempt for blues singers; Joe Smith's plunger
67.s: Musicians disliked accompanying blues singers until Joe Smith made it interesting with his plunger; the elite avoided Ma Rainey's rough crowd.
67.q: He did all his work with a plunger, behind this blues singer. Then the musicians started waking up to see how -- how it was a pleasure to play with the blues singers. That was done by Joe Smith.

67.t: Why male blues singers were neglected in the Black press
67.s: Cheatham recalls no popular male blues singers on stage, only guitar-playing singers in the South.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Now that may have been, but I don't remember any of them. I remember -- I have heard a lot of male blues singers in the South.

67.t: Playing for Bessie Smith in the Bijou pit
67.s: Cheatham played behind Bessie Smith when she lacked a pianist, and explains that TOBA singers were often so poor they could not carry accompanists.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: I played with Bessie Smith, sometimes she would have a piano, sometimes she didn't. It depended upon the finances. As I said before, lot of the blues singers when they could afford to carry pianos with them, they did. But sometimes they couldn't because they didn't have the money, they were in…

89.t: Mamie Smith's disastrous Pittsburgh opening with Bubber Miley
89.s: With Bubber Miley new to the stage, Mamie's costume trouble made the band repeat the introduction until her husband booted Bubber back on stage.
89.q: Originated in New York City, yes. I'll tell you, Johnny Dunn, the famous Johnny Dunn had quit so we hired Bubber Miley. I guess -- you know, he became very famous with Duke Ellington, and he had never been on stage before. And we opened in Pittsburgh, and Mamie had all new costumes made, and those…

89.t: Meeting Mamie Smith through Perry Bradford
89.s: Bradford heard him practicing behind his house, took him to meet Mamie Smith, and he recorded and then toured with her five-piece band.
89.q: It was just a record, two sides. Seventy-five cents. Yeah. Speaking about recording, the next session I did was with Mamie Smith and the way Peery Bradford heard me -- he was her manager then and also the writer of those tunes -- I lived at 130th Street and Peery lived directly behind me on 129th…

89.t: Daisey Martin and her Jazz Bellhops and four OKeh records
89.s: He rehearsed with Daisey Martin's group in bellhop uniforms and made about four records for OKeh in 1920, after Mamie Smith's first sides.
89.q: That was my first trip on -- actually on the stage outside of the circus, with a platform, more or less. And, then I met -- they said for me to come rehearse with another group called Daisey Martin and her Jazz Bellhops.

81.t: Bessie Smith in the studio and Edith Wilson's lesser recognition
81.s: Rasch asks about Handy and Bessie Smith's meticulousness; Johnson says Smith liked things just so, and that recognition depended on era.
81.ch: Telephone reels: blues and Bessie Smith
81.q: Well, she liked for things to be just about so and sound very good to my ears. And if you were one of the musicians, why -- and you didn't sound good to her, she would let you know. So -- because she had the sound of the blues (inaudible) and she liked (inaudible). That's about the whole thing.

81.t: His first song for Ethel Waters and meeting Bessie Smith
81.s: His first song, 'You Can't Do What My Last Man Did', was recorded by his friend Ethel Waters on Black Swan; Porter Grainger introduced him to Bessie Smith before 'Empty Bed Blues'.
81.ch: Reel 1: childhood, first songs, Fats Waller
81.q: We were friends -- we were friends long before she sang the song because just ordinary social strides among us -- I knew her so well and she knew me, and friends of hers and friends of mine, we were just socially okay, and so when it came to her recording, she was made to order for it.

81.t: The Ethel Waters record and 'Empty Bed Blues'
81.s: Johnson still has the original Ethel Waters record; Rasch asks about 'Empty Bed Blues' and the tape becomes untranscribable.
81.ch: Telephone reels: blues and Bessie Smith
81.q: I have the original record, I have it. (Inaudible) it came to me.

112.s: Wooding says Atlantic City audiences, who liked joyful or sentimental songs, did not appreciate Bessie Smith's blues.
112.ch: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
112.q: : Well, Bessie Smith was there and she did alright with the people, but a lot of people didn't appreciate Bessie Smith. Not because Bessie Smith wasn't a singer, but because they hadn't had a touch of the Blues.

112.t: Madhouse clientele and the coming of the blues
112.s: He says the Madhouse was a black-and-tan crowd, and that blues singers like Ma Rainey and Lucille Hegamin were coming into vogue.
112.ch: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
112.q: Yeah. It was like black and tan. See, and everybody held on together and everything was pretty good. A white party would sit down, a black party here, and all, you know, and they all -- they asked for everything at that time.

112.t: Crazy Blues, phonographs and wind-up records
112.s: He says Perry Bradford deserved the credit for Crazy Blues and that few Black households had wind-up phonographs.
112.ch: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
112.q: : Yes, it was a very big hit. But a lot of people don't give the right credit, to the right people. The man that's due credit is Perry Bradford.

258.t: A photograph of the young Bessie Smith
258.s: Thomas shows a picture of young Bessie Smith given him by a landlady who had Smith as a roomer; he never worked with her.
258.q: I've had one like that. I've had one like that. But here lately I use a Rudy Muck. Yeah. Now, this is a picture here. This is a very old picture. This picture here I think was made back in 1919. That's Bessie Smith.

258.t: The Ma Rainey on the Rabbit Foot Show and Big Mary
258.s: The Ma Rainey on the show was a Memphis woman, not the original from Columbus, Georgia; Big Mary also sang blues.
258.ch: Rabbit Foot show and show life
258.q: Well, there was a Ma Rainey. Used to work with the Rabbit Foot show, but it wasn't the original Ma Rainey. It wasn't the original? No, it was a Ma Rainey that lives in Memphis, Tennessee. Oh, yeah. See, this one came from- See, Ma Rainey originally from-

627.t: Ma Rainey, Memphis Minnie and a woman's blues song
627.s: Cage recalls Ma Rainey, seen or confused with another singer, and recites a blues about a woman whose man has left; the interviewer mentions Bessie Smith at Newport and Punch Miller playing the song.
627.ch: Cage on songs, cane work, records and family
627.q: Oh, that's late years, huh? Yeah. I thought it wasn't what I'm talking about. It wasn't Ramping Ma Rainey, but it put him in the mind.

627.t: Listening to Blind Lemon Jefferson and Bessie Smith records
627.s: Cage says he listened to all the blues singers on record, naming Blind Lemon Jefferson and Bessie Smith; the interviewer keeps their records.
627.ch: Cage on songs, cane work, records and family
627.q: Who did you listen to? I listened to Blind and that one's Jefferson. You know him? I got his records. Blind Lemon, huh? Yes. I got his records.

43.t: Ma Rainey, Mamie Smith and New Orleans blues singers
43.s: She worked on the same dates as Ma Rainey and heard the Smiths. She calls Mamie Smith's Crazy Blues the first popular blues record, and mentions Tilly Johnson and Ann Cook.
43.ch: Names, influences and early blues singers
43.q: Oh, yeah, I worked with Ma Rainey, like we played what you call day and date, you know. I was sure maybe, I was sure in one theater, her show in another theater like that, you know, see. Sure, I heard Ma Rainey, in fact, I heard them all, Bessie Smith, Clara Smith, Mamie Smith, you know. Who of…

43.t: Admired singers: Sophie Tucker and her sister the coon shouter
43.s: She went to hear Sophie Tucker at the Palace Theater and admired her sister's shouting and eye-rolling style.
43.ch: Names, influences and early blues singers
43.q: Well, the first singer that I would go every week to see when she was here was Sophie Tucker. She played at the Palace Theater here, and they used to charge 10 cents to go into Pitt. And on Saturdays, I'd hurry up and get my work through, so my mother would let me go up there to listen to her…

630.t: Bessie Smith compared with Ma Rainey
630.s: He heard Bessie Smith in person and compares her singing to Ma Rainey's heavier voice and stage actions.
630.q: Well she sang, Ma Rainey's voice was more heavy than Bessie's voice. See, Bessie was a good singer but Ma Rainey had a heavier voice. And which to my knowledge I believe Bessie Smith beat her singing. I think she beat her singing. But Ma Rainey, her voice was so loud and her actions was more, you…

630.t: Ma Rainey's songs and dances like the Frog
630.s: They discuss a Ma Rainey song, Fallin' Off the Log, and the Frog dance.
630.q: Well she'd make emotions, you know, like she was a gun in a hole or something like that, you know? And like she'd fallen off a log, all like that, you know? I was in motion, she was just good.

707.t: First recording singers heard: Mamie Smith, Edith Wilson, Ma Rainey
707.s: He recalls Mamie Smith and Edith Wilson and later played shows with Ma Rainey in Chicago.
707.q: Well, the first two blues singers that...I mean, two record...recording singers that I remember of ever hearing were Edith Wilson and Mamie Smith.

707.t: Favorite singers and pianists: Bessie Smith, Alonzo Johnson, Cooney Vaughn
707.s: He heard the classic blues stars, names Bessie Smith as favorite, dislikes Blind Lemon's timing, and rates Cooney Vaughn best pianist.
707.q: Oh, yeah. I heard her, I heard her around. Well, I heard, frankly, all of the people that traveled. I heard Bessie Smith, Mamie Smith. I saw them and, uh, Ida Cox and Ma Rainey and Butterbean and Susie. Mm-hmm. Well, I said, well, at the Lyric Theater, you used Ethel Waters, you'd see all of those.…

708.t: Blues singers versus popular and cafe singers
708.s: They sort singers (Bessie Smith, Ma Rainey, Ethel Waters, Alberta Hunter) into blues and popular types; she never worked with them since she was out of work 1927-34.
708.q: Let's see. That's kind of hard to figure out because in fact, they've been, it seemed like the blues was most popular, you know, for the records. and when my kind of singing came out it was something unusual, you know, and then the people seemed to like it, see, it was most unusual because the…

708.t: Nettie Compton and Bricktop as entertainers; how singers divided by idiom
708.s: They discuss whether Nettie and Bricktop sang blues, and Allen asks whether singers divided by idiom according to voice and education.
708.q: That's the first time I've seen Bricktop in my life. No, she didn't know Bricktop. Well, I tell you, Bricktop was, uh... I mean, she was a comedian... A kind of comedian. Comedian. Comedian, and, you know, sang, too, you know. So she's, um... Her best stock, though, is personality. Personality,…

3.t: Bessie Smith raised in her mother's house
3.s: Austin says Bessie Smith grew up with her and learned to sing by imitating Ma Rainey at a carnival.
3.q: Well, I worked with either London than I did anybody else, so I guess I would probably have to say that. But Maureen was a singer that, when I was a little girl...

3.s: They discuss Ida Cox, with whom Austin made records, and her death.
3.q: I read about it. And she lived in Nachter. Yeah, she lived down in there.

18.t: Mamie Smith and Bessie Smith's death
18.s: He recorded with Mamie Smith and Fletcher Henderson, and does not recall Bessie Smith's death.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: She was all right. I made a record with her too. Right here in New York, we made three recordings for different studios with Fletcher Henderson.

18.t: Fletcher Henderson and Bessie Smith in Atlanta, 1922
18.s: He first heard Fletcher Henderson's small group with Bessie Smith in Atlanta, around 1921-22.
18.ch: Family, Margaret's story and Eutris's memories
18.q: He had about 4 pieces in Atlanta. That's the first time I ever heard him play - Fletcher Henderson. ... Kaiser Marshall ... I don't know if he had a bass or not. I remember those three.

96.t: Sister Rosetta Tharpe and hearing Bessie Smith at Dreamland
96.s: Talk of gospel in entertainment leads to hearing Bessie Smith at Dreamland on the West Side with Bix and the gang.
96.q: Oh yes. Bix and I and all the Austin Highschool Gang, Benny Goodman and so forth. We used to go out and hear Bessie Smith at a place called Dreamland out on the West Side of Chicago. And she was something. But Ethel Waters to me, Ethel Waters sang you know.

96.t: Ethel Waters in 'Callico'; a record played
96.s: He praises Ethel Waters, recalls Bix taking him to see her sing 'I'm Coming Virginia', and plays the record.
96.q: I was going to say that Ethel Waters is a classic person and a musician. And anything she's done has been to me just beautiful.

6.t: Ma Rainey, Mamie Smith and the Lafayette
6.s: He doesn't recall hearing Bessie Smith, was unimpressed by Ma Rainey at the Lafayette, and mentions buying Mamie Smith records because Louis Armstrong played on them.
6.q: Look, I may have. I wouldn't say I hadn't, I didn't. I may have, but there was so much going on. There were so many people around in those days that I probably heard her. But I remember distinctly hearing Ma Rainey, because Ma Rainey was pretty popular in those days, and she was coming to the…

6.t: New York musicians' condescension toward Southern blues singers
6.s: Albertson relays Snowden, Wooding and Scott dismissing blues singers; Procope rejects this, saying Southern singers had a culture and accompanists were part of it, like Louis Armstrong.
6.q: Yeah, well, those are words, sophistication and whatever. But I always appreciated those people from the south, because they had a culture, and when they said, "My baby left me. My baby left me a mule to ride," or whatever, that was their culture. They were singing their hearts out, telling you,…

709.t: Careless Love, the nickname Preacher, reading in the string band
709.s: Chris was known for Careless Love and nicknamed Preacher, because women hollered for him to preach. The talk turns to string bands reading written music while also playing jazz by ear.
709.q: Yeah. He played that. He composed that piece. He composed that piece. He composed that piece. Oh, my God. Could this boy say that he's playing. That's Careless Love. And when he started playing that heavy ball, all of them women, they say, oh, preacher, preacher, preacher, preacher, preacher.…

251.t: Texas blues singers, Charlie Dixon and Bessie Smith
251.s: Albert says Texas blues singers did not sing opera and praises Charlie Dixon as a great man and bassist.
251.q: Charlie Dixon was one of the greatest men that I've met in my life. I wouldn't say he was the greatest musician, but he was truly a great man. And by the same token, he could play his bass and he could play his punk. He played with Singers Smith, which was another band that I didn't know, but…

34.t: Blues singers visiting New Orleans: Bessie Smith, Clara Smith, Ida Cox
34.s: He remembers seeing Bessie Smith's first visit and other blues singers, and mentions Louis Armstrong and Zutty Singleton.
34.q: No. She came. She went to some theater down there on Barone Street. It was a... I forget. It was a white theater. Hmm? It was right next to where the Lowe's, where the Lowe's theater was on Barone Street. Yeah. That was around 1914. Oh, that early. Yeah. Was she, did she have a piano player with…

710.s: Bailey recalls Alice, who sang blues by herself at the lake, and another female singer.
710.q: Mm-hmm. That was her name. You remember any of the songs you sang? No I didn't know him. I know where he was from downtown. From like a place.

711.t: Bessie Smith and hearing the blues in the South
711.s: She heard the blues in the South, was compared to Bessie Smith, and says she learned from her in time.
711.q: has meant something to you. Well, uh, in the South, in New Orleans where I was born, I didn't get a chance to hear, uh, the great singers like Roland Hayes and, and, um, uh, Grace Moore, Lily Pond, and all those great singers until I came to Chicago up north. Well, we, we did have a chance to hear…

712.t: A magazine clipping on blues and a letter from McIntyre
712.s: The interviewer notices a clipping about a blues magazine; she finds McIntyre's letter on a printing error.
712.q: I bet you it would show on the other side of that. Yeah. Well, now, there may be something in the written part that would indicate or something. Yeah, well, I'll, I'll.

275.t: Fats Waller and Bessie Smith in his repertoire
275.s: He sings Fats Waller and Bessie Smith numbers and says any blues or jazz tune can be done as coon shouting.
275.q: Oh yes, I have quite a bit of his records and I always liked his style of singing and I think he was a wonderful piano player. I liked his style of playing and his style of singing. I do a lot of his numbers called Why Am I Neglected and Honey Keep Your Mind On Me and Honeysuckle Rose and all those…

276.t: Learning 'Trouble Trouble' from Mamie Smith at Entertainer's Cabaret
276.s: Nash says he heard Mamie Smith sing 'Trouble Trouble' at Entertainer's Cabaret and sings it.
276.q: Where did you learn Trouble Trouble? Well, I heard that number at a place, Cabaret. They call it Entertainer's Cabaret. I heard Mamie Smith sing that song. Trouble Trouble. I've had it all my days.

44.t: Records Welch heard and Bessie Smith
44.s: Welch lists blues records he heard (Papa Charlie Jackson, Blind Lemon, Lonnie Johnson, Ma Rainey) and names Bessie Smith as favorite, claiming to have seen her sing in Mississippi.
44.q: she was a real good singer and then I knew her in personally she was raised up there on the syndicates at Scotts Mississippi and I was working at that sawmill at the time she used to give 4th of day July dances and she would she would stay she was staying there but the band would come from…

629.t: When the word jazz was first heard
629.s: The interviewer asks when people first used the word jazz; Picou wanders to the first woman to sing the blues on radio.
629.q: Yeah. Jazz can be... When... Let me see the great... The first woman that sang the blues. Ma Rainey? What? Ma Rainey? No. First woman that sang the blues to the television. To the television? Yeah. Oh.

12.s: He played behind Bessie Smith in Chicago, including a 1925 ball, but knows nothing of her private life.
12.q: Oh yes, I've heard Bessie Smith and had the pleasure to play behind her for a week. When I first came to Chicago to John King Olive, we played in the theater on 31st and State. Those times you didn't have any microphones. And I played a week with her. And later on in 25, she came back to Chicago to…

590.t: The best Armstrong period: the Hot Five; Billie Holiday and the blues singers
590.s: Alcorn praises the Hot Five as unmatched, and the talk turns to pattern-setting singers such as Billie Holiday, Bessie Smith and Ma Rainey.
590.q: Well, Louis had so many good, good, mixed in spots. Because I was crazy about, first thing everybody was crazy about the Hot Five. Never had another thing like that. Everybody tried to organize things, but they never got them close to the Hot Five. The Oriole and Johnny Giles. Yeah.

713.t: Favorite guitar players, playing blues, not singing
713.s: Nelson cannot recall the names of the guitarists he followed, says he mostly played blues, and never sang, having others sing for him.
713.q: the best of them I was here you know I don't know I forget the name of them sometimes the bits get a whole gang of me ball and see what I was one get out play one now yeah sometimes you know even know the name yeah that's right yeah that's right yeah playing with them what did you play mostly what…

714.t: Mahalia Jackson's style, comparisons, her death and her Dorsey album
714.s: The companion compares Mahalia's and Bessie Griffin's styles, and those of Joe May and Cleophus Robinson. Dorsey praises Mahalia's reach, describes his grief at her death, and the companion mentions her album of his songs.
714.q: Mahalia not only, she worked in everything, just the church, the lodge, wherever they wanted her to sing, and she sang her gospel songs, she was easy to get. And she loved to do it. Now the boy you just mentioned there, he's good, but he didn't get around as much as Mahalia.

288.s: Todd sang in a straight style with the band, years before Bessie Smith.
288.ch: Society work, Camilla Todd and Storyville
288.q: No, no. The only time we had that is when we was playing that Tom Anderson on Rampart and Canal. You remember Tom Anderson was the fellow who had all those big houses there in the district they used to call it.

128.t: Ma Rainey, Bessie Smith and women who ran their own groups
128.s: Asked about women blues singers, the men say they never worked with them; the singers had their own groups.
128.q: Talk about ruling. That's where they rule you at. Yeah, that's where it is. Incidentally, during your conversation, you've all talked about the boys with whom you've played, and the boys with whom you've brought out. Oh, excuse me. And you haven't mentioned some of the women who are supposed to…

197.t: Mamie Smith's voice and singer Sidney Hansel
197.s: How Mamie Smith sounded, her deep voice, the ten-piece band, and singer Sidney Hansel.
197.q: Well, she really sound good during that time. She did really good. She had a number she used to sing, Golf and Papa. Yeah. She really could sing that.

715.t: Playing behind blues singers for Williams
715.s: Allen backed many blues singers on Williams's dates, learned the style in New York, and was told to play rough rather than sweet.
715.q: Tooth Smith, Clarence Smith, Sarah Morton. I can't remember one of them. See, Clarence just recorded all those blues singers. So I used to go over there and play behind them. I made records, Jess Trumpet. Did you ever record with Ida Cox? No, I never recorded with Ida Cox. But you heard of her,…

317.t: The 'Three Generations of Blues' special with Sippie Wallace and Big Mama
317.s: The KPBS special at the Belly Up Tavern, in which Sippie Wallace and Big Mama Thornton fought on stage and Jeannie sang for the first time in front of Big Mama.
317.ch: Sippie Wallace and Big Mama Thornton
317.q: And I kind of, because I could see the cameras was on them you know. And I said, “You better get in there because it’ll never happen.”

640.t: Other singers and understanding Bessie Smith's lyrics
640.s: She admired Ethel Waters and Eva Taylor for diction; discusses unfamiliar phrases in Bessie's lyrics, John Hammond's music, and Bessie's non-Gospel voice.
640.ch: Growing up with jazz in northern England
640.q: Nobody ever really effected me like Bessie, but I was cognizant of other singers and one was Ethel Waters of course. I admired enormously Ethel Waters because she had great diction. If you’ll understand that I couldn’t understand what Ma Rainey was saying, and I had trouble with Bessie, I found…

670.s: Bessie Smith did not influence her; she heard those singers only later.
670.ch: Songs, singers and the state of jazz
670.q: No. My influences came from, I didn’t hear them at all until later on in the years. Because they started like talking about them. I don’t know exactly what year, but no. I had never

716.t: Firsts and certainty in music history: Crazy Blues and Dallas Blues
716.s: They discuss whether Crazy Blues was the first blues record, Marie Cahill's 1916 Dallas Blues, and why nothing in music history can be said absolutely.
716.q: Well she was a white lady but she was singing with a deep south accent that I do not think was contrived and the record was like a 12 inch record so there was a little opening monologue but she sang a full-length version of “Dallas Blues” and it’s not a bad performance.

68.t: Blues, Ma Rainey and 'Why Don't You Do Right'
68.s: Tate says blacks were leaving the blues while whites learned to sing them, and credits Ma Rainey with the tune later sung by Peggy.
68.q: They were singing the Blues, like Mamie Smith, Bessie Smith, Ma Rainey and all of them you know, and they were trying to get away from it. Like what was that other one [sings] If you had plenty money, like 1922, you wouldn’t be here, why don’t you do right like the other folk do, go out and give me…

26.s: Greer recalls recording with Bessie Smith and praises her sound.
26.q: I recorded a couple of times with her. But, I mean, she was very reserved. You know, she had a and like us guys, sidemen, we were sidemen. Like we'd play for her and that was it. Not socially.

167.s: He met B.B. King in San Francisco and thought him stuck up, but respects that King stuck with the blues.
167.q: And he was a kind of stuck up guy, you know. And I saw him back east somewhere. I've forgot the name of where I saw him, some town, back east, you know.

0.t: Mamie Smith compared with Bessie, Clara and Trixie Smith
0.s: Mamie was a smooth vaudeville singer who looked the part, not a blues shouter, and her fame owed to the first record and her agent.
0.ch: Mamie Smith and the New York dance bands
0.q: She was tops at that time, because, you know, they had three different Smith, and neither one of the four were ever related, but Mamie, Bessie -- of course, Bessie was the tops. There was Clara Smith. There was Trixie Smith.

70.t: Big Green, Bessie Smith and Dinah Washington's Play It Butter
70.s: Charlie Green played soulful blues on Bessie Smith's records; Jackson recorded Play That Slide Trombone with Dinah Washington, who called out his nickname.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Big Green. Big Green, there's nobody in this world I think could play blues as soulful as he could yet still turn around and play a most beautiful waltz you want to hear.

147.t: Favorite blues singers: Bessie Smith, Ma Rainey, Billie Holiday
147.s: Crawford names the blues singers he heard at the Palace Theatre and later ones such as Dinah Washington and Billie Holiday, and the rise of Sinatra.
147.q: My favorite blues singers? Well, the ones that came to the Palace Theatre in Memphis, when my aunt would take me. Ma Rainey, back in those days, Bessie Smith -- I read Bessie Smith had a gigantic sound as a singer.

91.t: The Bessie Smith playbill that never happened
91.s: Carter says he was billed with Bessie Smith but, per Hammond, she did not show up.
91.q: So you remember, we talked about this before and I couldn't remember ever having seen Bessie Smith in person, much less having appeared on a bill with her, and this same Playbill had also been in somebody else's book -- I'd been familiar with it for a number of years before the Chris Albertson book.

234.t: White rock performers copying Black artists: Joplin, Bessie Smith, Mae West
234.s: Johnston describes rock performers listening to Bessie Smith and Gil adds that Mae West built an act on Bessie Smith.
234.q: Well Mae West made a living of what she picked up off of Bessie Smith. Her style and all that kind of stuff. Mae West really picked that up and parlayed it into something.

29.t: Hearing Mamie Smith as a boy in Steubenville
29.s: Howard saw Mamie Smith in a Steubenville theater at ten or twelve with just a pianist, and she inspired him.
29.ch: Quality Serenaders, Cotton Club and union recollections
29.q: What's her name? Oh, she didn't play in no band. She had a band -- oh, shucks. She had a band and -- (Recording interruption)

418.t: First hearing the blues: Mamie, Bessie, Trixie and Clara Smith
418.s: He listened to the words of the blues singers named Smith, none of whom were related.
418.q: I don't know really. But I listened to the words of the Blues then. It was Mamie Smith I used to listen to, and Bessie Smith...and Trixie Smith, yeah... And there were some other Smiths then, too. There was a lot of Smiths...

386.t: Early blues singers and the mistaken 'Crazy Blues' record
386.s: The talk turns to Bessie Smith, Ida Cox and Ma Rainey, and Price tells how the Crazy Blues record he bought turned out to be Bert Williams.
386.q: Yeah, Ma Rainey and Bert Williams. Incidentally.....let me tell you a story. One time my mother...Mamie Smith had made "The Crazy Blues." It was a very, very popular thing. So they said...wanted me to go and buy "The Crazy Blues." Now, instead of my going to the black store to buy it, I went to the…

95.t: Who counts as a classic blues singer
95.s: Asked what classic blues means, she names a few women she considers classic singers and calls Bessie Smith a barrelhouse singer.
95.q: Well, she can, she can sing the blues. I saw Eva in New York. She tried -- Clarence made her a blues singer because he (unintelligible). And Eva then sing blues. She can sing blues like we can make you a blues singer. I'll make you a gospel singer, you (unintelligible).

611.t: Subbing with Mamie Smith's Jazz Hounds for Perry Bradford
611.s: The only blues-related work Waters recalls in Philadelphia is a one-off gig with Mamie Smith's Jazz Hounds arranged by Perry Bradford, and he explains why subbing jobs fade from memory.
611.ch: Other Philadelphia work and the union
611.q: Yeah, oh it was before, naturally before I went to Boston, see. 'Cause I went into Boston, I left directly the last band I worked with before I went to Boston was Charlie Miller, that's the last band, see. I rested, and then I went to New England.

31.t: Perry Bradford, Mamie Smith and Bessie Smith
31.s: Whaley confirms Perry Bradford discovered Mamie Smith, and recalls Bessie Smith at Carney's Inn.
31.q: Perry Bradford. I'm going to tell you, Perry Bradford was one of the originals. He discovered Mamie Smith, he had Mamie Smith.

428.t: Backing Bessie Smith at the Club Harlem
428.s: Hall recalls Bessie's last engagement, the middle-class view of blues, Ethel Waters and Marian Anderson, and not being impressed by her then.
428.ch: Philadelphia bands and the Club Harlem
428.q: Oh, no, no. I caught her live performance. My family took me to a vaudeville show when she was the featured singer. But you must understand, this was sinful music.

75.t: A weekend accompanying Bessie Smith in Binghamton
75.s: Through her husband he was hired to play for Bessie Smith, went by bus to Binghamton for a short, unhappy, inexperienced engagement with a broadcast, then talks about how much happened in New York.
75.ch: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
75.q: Right! Now, we're still in the Thirties. Remember, there was an old vocalist by the name of Bessie Smith. She was pretty fair/fat(?). And we had an elderly Jewish gentleman in there, you know...until I found out he was her husband! But I remember her.

97.s: Scott heard Bessie and Ethel Waters and liked them best.
97.q: Yes, yes, I heard Bessie. Bessie and Ethel Waters. That was the ones that I liked the best. Oh, she was great. She was (inaudible) before then. She was great, she could sing anything.

238.t: Rainey's fame, kindness and small band
238.s: She knew Rainey from records, found her kind to work with, and describes the four or five piece band behind her.
238.ch: Ma Rainey and the Palace Theater
238.q: In church I had, but I mean in this particular medium, you know, I had never -- I don't think I had. No, I know I hadn't. And particularly with a very world famous blues singer like Ma Rainey.

77.t: Rivalry with Bessie Smith's records; not listening to others
77.s: In 1923 they recorded the same numbers for different labels; Hunter says Bessie never had the chance to like her, and she did not listen to others' records but admired Bessie's voice.
77.ch: Records, Lovie Austin and a first marriage
77.q: I don't -- I don't think she disliked me. She didn't have a chance to like me or dislike me. But she just would -- she was just a woman just didn't bother, I guess, you know. I don't want to talk about her when she's

78.t: Ethel Waters and Fletcher's work for Black Swan
78.s: In LA Horace worked a Central Avenue club with Ethel Waters; he notes Fletcher started her out as music director for the Black Swan label with Clara Smith, Bessie Smith and Bert Williams.
78.ch: Army band, Lena Horne, Billie Holiday and the 1950s
78.q: : I got a job down there working at a club right on Central Avenue, and I'll tell you another lady was on the bill -- Ethel Waters was the star attraction. So this could go on. But these things happened. It sounds like fairy tales, but it really happened.
